title: The guest is a god
hookLine: people who own almost nothing still host three guests as if they were gods
carry: atithi devo bhava: the guest is god

lines: YOU WILL SIT. YOU WILL BE FED.
cards: At a grandmother's house, in India and plenty of other places, a visitor's rules are old ones. You will sit. You will be given water.
You will be fed, hungry or not, and you will not be allowed to help with the dishes. The sages of Dandaka own almost nothing: a hut, a water pot, the bark they wear.
And the first thing they do for Rama, Sita and Lakshmana is exactly that.

teach.b: In the Ramayana, hospitality is almost a rite of its own.
When a guest comes to a hermitage, the hosts offer water to wash the feet, water for the hands and mouth, a seat, and food, usually fruit and roots, whatever the forest gives.
The Sanskrit word for a guest is atithi. One old explanation reads it as the one who comes without a date, the visitor you didn't plan for.

teach.h: ATITHI DEVO BHAVA: TREAT THE GUEST AS A GOD.
teach.b: And the Taittiriya Upanishad gives a teacher's parting words to a student, among them a line still quoted today: treat the guest as a god, atithi devo bhava.
It sits beside honoring your mother, your father and your teacher. So when the sages spread grass for the travelers and bring them what they have, they aren't just being polite.
They're keeping a duty as serious as their prayers. Many Hindu homes still live by it: water and food before any talk, whether the guest is family or the man who came to fix the sink.
Rama spends the night, rested and honored.
At sunrise he takes his leave and walks on, deeper into Dandaka. Valmiki lets you feel the change. The ring of huts falls behind.
The trees close in. The forest grows dense and loud with crickets, full of wild animals, with pools half dried and no paths.
The sages' welcome is the last soft place for a while. Welcome first, then the wild. Out of that thick forest, the third book's first danger is coming.

how: Hindu households often welcome a guest with water, a seat and food before conversation, and the Upanishad's line atithi devo bhava, treat the guest as a god, is still quoted.

games.q: you're a forest sage with a hut and a water pot. three tired travelers arrive. what do you do first?
o: ask who they are and what they want.
offer water, a seat and food.
point them to the next hermitage.
games.why: the sages welcome them as guests should be welcomed, and Rama rests there for the night.

practice: Remember a time someone welcomed you when you arrived tired, and the moment you were handed something: water, tea, a seat.
Feel how your body relaxed, then picture being the one who offers it; breathe in being welcomed, and breathe out welcoming.

wordCard.voice: The sages. They host Rama with water, a seat and forest food, keeping the old duty: treat the guest as a god.

orig.note: Sanskrit atithi: a guest. a traditional explanation reads it as 'one without a fixed date' (a-tithi).

carryVoice: Your line: atithi devo bhava, the guest is god. The sages' welcome is the last soft place before the forest closes in. That's day five hundred fifty-two.
